Equated by the Romans with the Greek goddess Athena, this member of the Capitoline Triad favors an owl as her sacred creature — who is she?

A former physics teacher turned politician, this four-term Turkish MP ran as the main opposition's presidential candidate in 2018, finishing second to the incumbent with just over 30% of the vote — who is he?
Muharrem İnce: Turkish politician. Muharrem İnce (Turkish: [inˈdʒe]; born 4 May 1964) is a Turkish physics teacher, school principal, sport executive, and politician.

Serving as Turkey's 23rd prime minister from 1996 to 1997, this Islamist politician was later banned from politics for violating the constitution's secularism clause after founding a movement called Millî Görüş — who is he?
Necmettin Erbakan: Prime Minister of Turkey from 1996 to 1997.
Founded by Nayib Bukele in 2017, this party now holds near-unanimous control of El Salvador's Legislative Assembly — which party?
Nuevas Ideas: Political party in El Salvador. Nuevas Ideas (English: New Ideas; abbreviated N or NI) is the current ruling political party of El Salvador.
Hebrew for 'Jewish Power,' this far-right Israeli political party grew out of the banned Kach movement and was linked in its early years to politician Itamar Ben-Gvir — which party?
Otzma Yehudit: Israeli far-right political party. Otzma ran independently in the 2013 election and as part of a list with ultra-Orthodox party Yachad in 2015.
Based on the doctrine of a 20th-century Argentine leader, this political movement is defined by three 'flags' — social justice, economic independence, and political sovereignty — what is it called?
Peronism: Argentine political movement. Peronism, also known as justicialism, is an Argentine ideology and political movement, based on the ideas, doctrine, and legacy of Juan Perón (1895–1974).

The first person from West Bengal to become President of India, this longtime Congress leader had been Finance Minister just before his 2012 election and was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2019. Who is he?
Pranab Mukherjee: President of India from 2012 to 2017. Prior to his election as President, Mukherjee was Finance Minister from 2009 to 2012 also in 1982 to 1984.
This Indian politician became Minister of Defence in 2019 and was the first person born after independence to serve as Union Minister of Home Affairs — who is he?
Rajnath Singh: Defense Minister of India since 2019.
Going by his initials 'rms,' this programmer launched the GNU Project, founded the Free Software Foundation, and wrote every version of the GNU General Public License — who is he?
Richard Stallman: American activist and programmer (born 1953)
Orphaned of his murdered father at age two, this Shia cleric grew up to lead a revolution that toppled the Shah and made him his country's first supreme leader — who was he?
Ruhollah Khomeini: Supreme Leader of Iran from 1979 to 1989.
This French economist and Green party lawmaker, representing a Paris constituency since 2022, became a leading voice of France's version of the Me Too movement — who is she?
Sandrine Rousseau: French economist and politician. Rousseau previously served as a vice-president of the University of Lille.
At 35, he became Russia's youngest-ever prime minister in 1998 and later ran the Rosatom nuclear agency for over a decade — who is this Kremlin technocrat?
Sergey Kiriyenko: Prime Minister of Russia In 1998.
A Jagiellonian king of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1506, he earned his "the Old" nickname only later, to tell him apart from the son who succeeded him. Who was this monarch?
Sigismund I the Old: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1506 to 1548. Sigismund was born in the town of Kozienice in 1467 as the fifth son of Casimir IV and Elizabeth of Austria.
The only prime minister to date from the modern Conservative Party of Canada, this Calgary economist co-founded the party and led the country from 2006 to 2015 — who is he?
Stephen Harper: Prime Minister of Canada from 2006 to 2015. Stephen Joseph Harper (born April 30, 1959) is a Canadian politician who served as the 22nd prime minister of Canada from 2006 to 2015.
Its Sanskrit name evokes weaving or a loom, and this occult Hindu tradition views the body as divine, seeking the union of the god Shiva and his consort — what is it called?
Tantra: Esoteric traditions of Hinduism and Buddhism.
Around the year 1010, this Icelandic explorer followed Leif Eriksson's route to Vinland with his wife Gudrid in a short-lived bid to found a permanent settlement — who was he?
Serving as ealdorman of Northumbria from 1006 until his assassination in 1016, this ruler's death sparked a blood feud with Thurbrand the Hold — who was he?
This Hungarian lawyer-politician has led the Fidesz party and served as prime minister twice, taking the country into NATO during his first stint. Who is he?
Viktor Orbán: Prime Minister of Hungary (1998–2002, 2010–2026)
This early American writer gave us 'Rip Van Winkle' and 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,' and later served as the U.S. ambassador to Spain — who was he?
Washington Irving: American writer, historian and diplomat (1783–1859)
The only Democrat elected president during the Republican-dominated Progressive Era, he steered the U.S. through World War I and championed the League of Nations — which 28th president was he?
Woodrow Wilson: President of the United States from 1913 to 1921.
A close associate of Gandhi and a founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, this Berlin-educated educationist rose to become president of India, dying in office in 1969 — who was he?
Zakir Husain: President of India from 1967 to 1969.
Which of these people was born first?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Jabir ibn Hayyan (born 721) is the earliest of the four. The c. 215 treatises that survive today mainly deal with alchemy and chemistry, magic, and Shi'ite religious philosophy.
Which of these four has been around longest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Dorothea Klumpke is an astronomer. Dorothea Klumpke Roberts (August 9, 1861 in San Francisco – October 5, 1942 in San Francisco) was an American astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Georg Cantor is a mathematician. Cantor's method of proof of this theorem implies the existence of an infinity of infinities.
What is the atomic number of Thorium?
Thorium is a chemical element; it has symbol Th and atomic number 90.
What is the atomic number of Osmium?
Osmium (from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) 'smell') is a chemical element; it has symbol Os and atomic number 76.
In what year was Scott Cawthon born?
Scott Cawthon: Cawthon began his career developing family-friendly Christian video games to minimal success.
In what year was Brian Cox born?
Brian Cox (physicist): Brian Edward Cox (born 3 March 1968) is an English physicist and musician.
In what year was Nikola Tesla born?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
In what year did Homi J. Bhabha die?
Homi J. Bhabha: Bhabha was awarded the Adams Prize (1942) and Padma Bhushan (1954), and nominated for the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1951 and 1953–1956.
In what year did Enrico Fermi die?
Enrico Fermi: With his colleagues, Fermi filed several patents related to the use of nuclear power, all of which were taken over by the US government.
In what year was Beryllium discovered?
Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
Eurocopter Tiger: Airbus Helicopters. The Eurocopter EC665 Tiger, is a four-blade, twin-engine attack helicopter which first entered service in 2003.
In which country is Harrier jump jet?
Harrier jump jet: United Kingdom. The Harrier emerged as the only truly successful V/STOL design of the many attempted during that era.
Fufu: Ghana. Fufu (or fufuo, foofoo, foufou foo-foo) is a pounded meal found in West African cuisine.
Who is credited with discovering Tennessine?
Tennessine: Yuri Oganessian. Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.
Who is credited with discovering Ammonia?
Ammonia: Joseph Priestley. Ammonia is an inorganic chemical compound of nitrogen and hydrogen with the formula NH3.
Who is credited with discovering Selenium?
Selenium: Jöns Jacob Berzelius. Selenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Se and atomic number 34.
A King's College Cambridge graduate who earned a Princeton doctorate in 1938, he later joined Britain's wartime codebreaking effort and pioneered theoretical computing — who was he?
Alan Turing (23 June 1912 - 7 June 1954) was an English mathematician, computer scientist, logician, cryptanalyst, philosopher and theoretical biologist.
Despite overseeing Soviet thermonuclear weapons development, this physicist won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize for his activism on human rights and individual freedom — who is he?
Andrei Sakharov (21 May 1921 - 14 December 1989) was a Soviet physicist and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, which he was awarded in 1975 for emphasizing human rights around the world.
Excavated in Argentina starting in 1989 under paleontologist José Bonaparte, this Late Cretaceous titanosaur weighed as much as 80 tons — which genus of giant sauropod?
Argentinosaurus (meaning "lizard from Argentina") is a genus of giant sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.

Originating in Central Africa and classified as a hound by the American Kennel Club, this dog breed doesn't bark but instead makes an unusual yodel-like sound due to its uniquely shaped larynx — what's the breed?
Basenji is a breed of hunting dog created from stock that originated in Central Africa, including in the Republic of the Congo and other adjacent tropical African countries.
A flowering vine native to South Asia, this plant's small dried red drupes become the world's most traded spice, its final coloring depending on how ripe the fruit was when harvested — which spice?
Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is a flowering vine in the family Piperaceae, cultivated for its fruit (the peppercorn), which is usually dried and used as a spice and seasoning.
Also known as undulant fever and Malta fever, this zoonotic illness spreads mainly through drinking unpasteurized milk and is caused by tiny coccobacilli — what is it?
Brucellosis is a zoonosis (zoonotic disease) spread primarily via ingestion of unpasteurized milk from infected animals.

Once thought to not really exist as a stable molecule, this compound was confirmed since around 1990 to have a real, if fleeting, existence — lasting only about 20 milliseconds at body temperature — what compound is it?
Carbonic acid is a chemical compound with the chemical formula H2CO3.

This perennial flowering herb is the only species of its onion-relative genus native to both the New World and Old World, prized for its edible leaves and flowers and also used to repel insects. What herb is this?
Chives is a species of flowering plant in the family Amaryllidaceae.
Part of the same species as cabbage and broccoli, this loose-leafed member of the 'kale group' has been grown for its big, dark-green leaves since classical antiquity — what is it?
Collard (plant) is a group of loose-leafed cultivars of Brassica oleracea (the same species as many common vegetables, including cabbage and broccoli).
Together with birds, this order of predatory reptiles is one of only two survivors of the ancient Archosauria — and it lumps together alligators, caimans, and gharials. What is it?
Crocodilia is an order of semiaquatic, predatory reptiles that are known as crocodilians.

Named from the Latin word for 'finger' because of its tubular, spike-borne flowers, this genus of about 20 European and West Asian species was reclassified into a new plant family in 2001 — what is it commonly called?
Digitalis (or) is a genus of about 20 species of herbaceous perennial plants, shrubs, and biennials, commonly called foxgloves.
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints, stretchy velvety skin, and abnormal scarring, sometimes leading to aortic dissection — name the condition?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS) are a group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders.
From abortion to animal welfare to business practices, the 'applied' branch of this philosophical study tackles real-world moral problems. What is it?
Ethics is the philosophical study of moral phenomena. Its main branches include normative ethics, applied ethics, and metaethics.
This everyday bodily process — expelling gas from the intestines through the anus — has its own dedicated field of scientific study named after it: what's the term for the process itself?
Flatulence is the expulsion of gas from the intestines via the anus, commonly referred to as farting.
Its name comes from Greek words meaning "study of the earth," and this science examines the rocks and processes that shape not just our planet but other astronomical bodies too — what field is it?
Geology is a branch of natural science concerned with the Earth and other astronomical bodies, the rocks of which they are composed, and the processes by which they change over time.
Nicknamed the 'benevolent dictator for life' of the language he invented, this Dutch programmer relinquished that title in July 2018. Who is he?
Guido van Rossum (born 31 January 1956) is a Dutch programmer.
This genus of the mallow family includes several hundred species prized for their large, showy blooms, and is sometimes known by the alternate name rose mallow — name the genus?
Hibiscus is a genus of common flowering plants in the mallow family, Malvaceae.
This medical condition occurs when the body, or a region of it, is deprived of adequate oxygen at the tissue level — what is it called?

Hypoxia (medicine) is a condition in which the body or a region of the body is deprived of an adequate oxygen supply at the tissue level. Hypoxia may be classified as either generalized, affecting the whole body, or local, affecting a region of the body.

Once found as far north as Texas's Lower Rio Grande Valley but now extirpated from the US, this slender wild cat comes in gray and red color morphs, ranging from Mexico to Argentina — what animal is it?
Jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi); or is a wild cat native to the Americas.
This mammalogist survived a 3,000-meter fall strapped to her airplane seat after a 1971 lightning strike, then spent 11 days alone in the Amazon before rescue — who is she?
Juliane Koepcke (born 10 October 1954), is a German-Peruvian mammalogist who specialises in bats.
Native to the Mediterranean and prized for its fragrant purple blooms, this genus of some 47 flowering plant species belongs to the sage family — name it?
Lavandula (common name lavender) is a genus of 47 known species of perennial flowering plants in the sage family, Lamiaceae.

This American single-engine supersonic interceptor, designed by Kelly Johnson after interviewing Korean War fighter pilots, became part of the 'Century Series' and was widely used as a Cold War fighter-bomber. What is it?
Lockheed F-104 Starfighter is an American single-engine, supersonic interceptor. It was also produced under license by other nations and saw widespread service outside the United States.
A large canine of South America resembling a red fox in markings but being neither fox nor wolf. It's the only species in its genus and the largest canine in South America. What is it?
Maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus) is a large canine of South America.
Discovered in 1893 and existing as two enantiomers, this CNS stimulant is best known in its hydrochloride salt form as 'crystal meth' — what is it?

Methamphetamine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant that is primarily used as a recreational or performance-enhancing drug and less commonly as a second-line treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
Their name means "little fly" in Spanish, and biologists class them as micropredators — all sip flower nectar, but the females of many species also drink blood. What are they?
Mosquito are a family of small flies consisting of 3,600 species.
Named for a pioneering physicist's work on classical mechanics, this SI unit of force equals the push needed to accelerate one kilogram at one metre per second squared — name the unit?
Newton (unit) (symbol: N) is the unit of force in the International System of Units (SI).

Physicians in this medical specialty diagnose and surgically treat eye disorders — and can often spot signs of diseases elsewhere in the body just by examining a patient's eyes — what specialty is it?
Ophthalmology is the branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis, treatment, and surgery of eye diseases and disorders.
This Scottish biologist-turned-town-planner coined the word 'conurbation' and his work contains one of the earliest versions of 'think globally, act locally.' Who was he?
Patrick Geddes (2 October 1854 - 17 April 1932) was a Scottish biologist, sociologist, Comtean positivist, geographer, philanthropist and pioneering town planner.

First described in 1850, this family of over 2,000 araneomorph spiders includes the cellar spider and the "vibrating spider" — and lends the nickname "daddy long-legs" to one of its species; what is the family?
Pholcidae are a family of araneomorph spiders. The family, first described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, is divided into 94 genera.

First domesticated by ancient peoples of the Iranian plateau roughly 5,000 years ago, this deciduous shrub bears a fruit rich in symbolic and mythological meaning across many cultures — name the fruit?
Pomegranate (Punica granatum) is a fruit-bearing, deciduous shrub in the family Lythraceae, subfamily Punicoideae, that grows to between 1.5-5 metres (5-16 ft) tall.
Ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius believed this oratorical skill could profoundly move even those not present in the room — what is the term for addressing a live audience?
Public speaking is the delivery of a speech to a live audience.
This long-term autoimmune disorder leaves joints warm, swollen and painful — typically the same ones on both sides of the body — and can stiffen worse after rest. What is it?
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-term autoimmune disorder that primarily affects joints.

Native to the Azores, Europe, and the Middle East, this tree or shrub's flowers and berries have long been used for cordial and wine, and it also appears in traditional medicine and dietary supplements — name this plant?
Sambucus nigra is a temperate species of tree or shrub in the family Viburnaceae native to the Azores, Europe, and the Middle East.
Before becoming the first woman on Facebook's board, this executive ran global sales at Google and assisted Lawrence Summers at the World Bank — who later wrote 'Lean In'?
Sheryl Sandberg (born August 28, 1969) is an American technology executive, philanthropist and writer.
This leafy green vegetable's high oxalate content gives raw and cooked versions noticeably different flavors, with blanching helping to tone it down — what vegetable is it?
Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy green flowering plant native to Central and Western Asia.
This South African biologist established the tiny roundworm C. elegans as a model organism, work that helped earn him a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Who was he?
Sydney Brenner (13 January 1927 - 5 April 2019) was a South African biologist.
Raised in Michigan with little schooling, he sold his first inventions by age 22 and moved to New York to chase engineering — going on to become one of America's most famous inventors. Who?
Thomas Edison (February 11, 1847 - October 18, 1931) was an American inventor and businessman.
Native to Central and South America but now found in sub-Saharan Africa, which parasitic flea burrows into skin to cause the condition tungiasis?
Tunga penetrans is a species of flea also known as the jigger, jigger flea, chigoe, chigo, chigoe flea, chigo flea, nigua, sand flea, or burrowing flea.

Commanding the first spaceflight to carry multiple crew members in 1964, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first human to die during a space mission when his capsule's parachute failed on reentry in 1967 — who was he?
Vladimir Komarov (16 March 1927 - 24 April 1967) was a Soviet test pilot, aerospace engineer, and cosmonaut.
Which East Asian citrus fruit, believed to have originated in central China as a hybrid of mandarin orange and ichang papeda, is now also grown in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe?
Yuzu (Citrus junos, from Japanese or) is a citrus fruit and plant in the family Rutaceae of Chinese origin.
Native to Africa and Yemen, this drought-resistant tree species has individuals radiocarbon-dated to over 1,275 years old — what is it?
Adansonia digitata: Species of plant native to Africa.
Brother of a concert pianist and son of an astronomer, this Russian mathematician built the foundational theory of stability in dynamical systems — who was he?
Formed when ammonia gains an extra hydrogen ion, this positively charged molecule, NH4+, is a key player in the global nitrogen cycle — what is it?
Bridging biology and sociology, this scientific study of humanity has social, cultural, linguistic and biological branches, and treats archaeology as the study of the human past — what's the field?
Anthropology: Scientific study of humans, human behavior, and societies.
This Russian designer and outspoken blogger, known for provocative and often obscene commentary, founded a namesake design studio and is a descendant of the Tolstoy family — who is he?
Artemy Lebedev: Russian designer and businessman (born 1975)
Sold as Zithromax, this antibiotic tackles strep throat, pneumonia and traveler's diarrhea — but its tendency to cause QT prolongation keeps doctors watchful of the heart. Which drug is it?
Azithromycin: Antibiotic. It is administered by mouth, into a vein, or as topical treatment for the eye.
Commonly known as barberry, this genus of deciduous and evergreen shrubs grows worldwide except Australia, and one of its species is Oregon's official state flower — what genus is it?
Berberis: Genus of flowering plants representing the barberry family.
This North American wild cat earns its name from the black-tipped, stubby tail it sports, along with distinctive black bars on its forelegs — one of the four species of lynx. Which animal is it?
Bobcat: Medium-sized North American wild cat.

After resigning from Evergreen State College following 2017 protests over campus racial equity, this podcaster and former evolutionary biology professor was named part of the 'intellectual dark web' — who is he?
Bret Weinstein: American podcaster and author (born 1969)
This highly soluble white crystalline salt is spread on icy roads for de-icing and, in its anhydrous form, works as a moisture-absorbing desiccant. What compound is it?
Calcium chloride: Chemical compound. The compound is a white crystalline solid at room temperature, and it is highly soluble in water.
Native to the Mediterranean, this legume tree's seed pods are ground into a chocolate substitute, while its seeds yield a common food thickener known as locust bean gum — which tree?
Carob: Small tree grown for its edible pods and landscaping.
This goat-antelope roams mountain ranges from the Pyrenees to the Caucasus and has even been introduced to New Zealand's South Island — which animal?
Named after a 17th-century English physician, this ring-shaped network of arteries supplies blood to the brain in humans and other vertebrates — what is it called?
Circle of Willis: Circulatory anastomosis that supplies blood to the brain and surrounding structures.
Also known as foremilk or historically as 'beestings,' this early substance produced by mammary glands right after birth delivers antibodies and immune factors to newborns. What is it?
Colostrum: Form of milk produced immediately following the delivery of newborn.
Latin for 'raven,' this widely distributed bird genus includes crows and rooks and gave a group of its members the eerie collective noun 'a murder' — what genus is it?
Corvus: Genus of birds including crows, ravens and rooks.

First synthesized in 1874, this insecticide earned its discoverer a 1948 Nobel Prize and was used in WWII against malaria and typhus before becoming infamous for its environmental damage — what is it?
DDT: Organochloride known as an insecticide.

This group of microalgae generates roughly a fifth to a half of Earth's oxygen each year, and its dead shells drift on Saharan winds to fertilize the entire Amazon basin with millions of tons of dust annually. What are they?
Diatom: Single-celled alga with a silica cell wall.
Smaller and shorter-necked than their swan and goose cousins in the family Anatidae, these aquatic birds are often confused with grebes, loons, and coots — what are they?
Duck: Common name for many species of bird.
The first woman admitted to MIT, this environmental chemist was the first to apply chemistry to nutrition and founded the home economics movement — who was she?
Ellen Swallow Richards: American engineer and chemist (1843–1911)
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics and helps maintain reproductive tissues from puberty through pregnancy — what is it?
This front-of-the-head body part houses most sense organs — eyes, nose, and mouth — and its damage or scarring can profoundly affect a person's sense of identity. What is it?
Face: Front of a head. The face is the front of the head in humans and many other animals that features most of the sense organs including the eyes, nose and mouth.
Belonging to a bird family that's the only survivor of its order, this wading bird comes in four American species plus two more across Africa and Eurasia — what is it?
Flamingo: Family of birds. There are four flamingo species distributed throughout the Americas (including the Caribbean), and two species native to Afro-Eurasia.
Sold under the brand name Lasix, this loop diuretic treats edema from heart failure and kidney disease and can also cause tinnitus and light sensitivity?

Furosemide: Loop diuretic medication. Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a loop diuretic medication used to treat edema due to heart failure, liver scarring, or kidney disease.
Endemic to China and sporting a handy 'thumb' on its forepaw to grip bamboo, this black-and-white bear weighs in around 100 to 115 kg — what animal is it?
Giant panda: Species of bear. The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), also known as the panda bear or simply panda, is a bear species endemic to China.
Sporting pied black-and-white plumage with a red patch on its lower belly, this Palearctic bird drums on trees to mark territory and excavate nest holes — which species?
Great spotted woodpecker: Species of bird. The great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major) is a medium-sized woodpecker with pied black and white plumage and a red patch on the lower belly.
Caused by mutations in the ABCA12 gene, this severe genetic skin disorder covers newborns in thick, cracked plates resembling armor — what is it?
Harlequin-type ichthyosis: Genetic skin disease. Harlequin-type ichthyosis is a genetic disorder that results in thickened skin over nearly the entire body at birth.

Bred by Polynesians in the pre-Columbian era from two Pacific island species, this tropical flowering plant is the national flower of Malaysia and the unofficial national flower of Haiti — what is it?
Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis: Hybrid species of flowering plant. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant in the tropics and subtropics.
Carl Wilhelm Scheele pinned down this gas's composition in 1777; it's flammable, smells of rotten eggs, and kills by blocking cellular respiration much like cyanide — what colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen sulfide: Poisonous and flammable gas. Hydrogen sulfide (preferred IUPAC name and American English) or hydrogen sulphide (Commonwealth English) is a chemical compound with the formula H2S.

Named for the indigo-blue line seen in its spectrum when discovered in 1863, this soft, silvery-white metal with atomic number 49 is used to make the transparent conductive coating on flat-panel displays — what is it?
Indium: Chemical element with atomic number 49 (In)
An English mathematician who shaped matrix and invariant theory, he founded the American Journal of Mathematics while leading the field at Johns Hopkins — who was he?
Hailed as a 'miracle worker' in 1955, this researcher refused to patent his polio vaccine so it could spread worldwide for free — who is he?
Jonas Salk: American inventor of the polio vaccine (1914–1995)
A German mechanical engineer turned economist, he founded a famous annual gathering of global leaders in 1971 and chaired it until stepping down in 2025. Who is he?
Klaus Schwab: Founder of the World Economic Forum (born 1938)

Named from the Greek word for 'honey bee' because its flowers attract them, this citrus-scented herb in the mint family has been cultivated since at least the 16th century for tea and aromatic oils — what is it?

Three of this crustacean's five pairs of legs bear claws, with the first pair often dramatically oversized, and its burrow-dwelling relatives include the Norway variety known as langoustine - which creature?
Lobster: Family of clawed marine crustaceans.
With deeply forked tails and iridescent, tiger-like stripes on their backs, these pelagic fish migrate in huge schools to shallow coastal spawning grounds — what are they?
Mackerel: Pelagic fish. Mackerel is a common name applied to a number of different species of pelagic fish, mostly from the family Scombridae.
This American psychologist completed every requirement for a Harvard Ph.D. in 1895 but was denied the degree because of her gender — who was she?
Mary Whiton Calkins: American philosopher and psychologist. In 1903, Calkins was the twelfth in a listing of fifty psychologists with the most merit, chosen by her peers.

From a Greek word meaning 'change,' this term covers the enzyme-driven reactions that turn food into usable energy and building blocks while excreting waste — letting organisms grow and reproduce. What is it?
Metabolism: Set of chemical reactions in organisms.
This industry extracts everything from coal and gemstones to rock salt and gravel from the Earth, but is also linked to land degradation and habitat loss — what is it?
Mining: Extraction of valuable minerals or other geological materials from the Earth.
This contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease is best known for causing painful swelling of the glands beside the jaw — its hallmark symptom. What is it?
Mumps: Human disease caused by paramyxovirus.
Discovered in 1885 by Carl Auer von Welsbach, this rare-earth element tarnishes quickly in air and produces pink, purple, and yellow compounds when oxidized — which element, atomic number 60?
Neodymium: Chemical element with atomic number 60 (Nd)

A French apothecary and physician who studied at Avignon until the plague closed it, he's far better remembered for 942 cryptic quatrains said to foretell the future — by what Latinised name is he known?
Nostradamus: French apothecary, astrologer and seer (1503–1566)
Sold under the brand name Tamiflu, this oral antiviral is recommended for high-risk patients within 48 hours of their first flu symptoms. What drug is it?
Oseltamivir: Antiviral medication used against influenza.
Believed to have originated in Sardinia and first cultivated in Britain in 1548, which herb is often used simply as a garnish today?
Parsley: Species of flowering plant in the celery family Apiaceae cultivated as an herb.
Smaller than 3 millimetres and caused by leaking capillaries, these tiny red or purple skin spots can be forensically significant when found around the eyes or neck — what are they called?
Petechia: Small red or purple blemish on the skin, eyes, etc. due to rupture of capillaries.

The most economically important member of the bromeliad family, this South American fruit became a 17th-century European symbol of luxury — and forms when many small flowers fuse into one — what is it?
Pineapple: Species of flowering plant in the family Bromeliaceae.
This deliquescent white salt helps make Dutch-process cocoa, soap, and glass, and can also turn up leaking from old alkaline batteries — what compound?
Potassium carbonate: Chemical compound. It is a white salt, which is soluble in water and forms a strongly alkaline solution.

Marked by delusions, hallucinations and disorganized thinking, this state — not a diagnosis itself — often stems from schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or alcohol-related brain damage — what is it called?
Psychosis: Abnormal condition of the mind.
Also called broccoli rabe, this bitter, vitamin K-rich cruciferous vegetable is a Mediterranean cuisine staple with edible leaves, buds, and stems — what is it?
This blue supergiant in Orion, also known as Beta Orionis, outshines the Sun by up to 363,000 times and anchors a system of at least four stars — which star?
